reason: The sources provide rich, cross-verified details across multiple independent sites documenting the cosmic timeline from stellar extinction to black hole evaporation.
story: Right now, we live in the Stelliferous Era, the golden age of starlight. But the universe is on a one-way trip toward total darkness. Driven by dark energy, space is accelerating outward, pushing distant galaxies forever out of view. In about 100 trillion years, the last hydrogen fuel will be spent, and star formation will shut down forever. The longest-lasting stars, frugal red dwarfs, will fade into dead black dwarfs. All remaining ordinary matter will be locked into cooling stellar remnants: white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes. Then, even black holes will meet their end. Through Hawking radiation, black holes slowly bleed away their mass, growing hotter until they vanish. By roughly a googol years from now—a one followed by 100 zeros—even the supermassive titans will evaporate. All that remains is an unimaginably cold, dilute sea of stray subatomic particles where no energy can flow and nothing will ever happen again.
angle: Even black holes are not permanent: over a googol years, they will all slowly evaporate into radiation, leaving the universe completely empty and dark forever.

claims.claim: The ultimate cooling and thermodynamic equilibrium of the universe is popularly known as the Big Freeze, Big Chill, or heat death.
In 1998, observations of distant Type Ia supernovae revealed that dark energy is driving the universe to expand at an accelerating rate.
William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) formulated the concept of universal energy dissipation and heat death in the 1850s using the laws of thermodynamics.
Within roughly two trillion years, the accelerating expansion will redshift distant galaxies outside our local grouping so severely that they will become completely undetectable.
In approximately 100 trillion (10^14) years, all star formation will cease as available gas is exhausted, ending the Stelliferous Era.
Low-mass red dwarf stars are the longest-living stars in the cosmos, burning their nuclear fuel for up to 10 trillion years.
Once red dwarfs exhaust their hydrogen fuel, they will cool into dormant stellar remnants known as black dwarfs.
During the Degenerate Era, the dominant remaining stellar-mass objects will be brown dwarfs, white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes.
If two carbon-oxygen white dwarfs collide with a combined mass above the Chandrasekhar limit of about 1.4 solar masses, they ignite a Type Ia supernova, briefly illuminating the dark universe.
Black holes do not last forever; they slowly lose mass and evaporate by emitting Hawking radiation.
As an evaporating black hole loses mass, its temperature and luminosity rise rather than drop.
Supermassive black holes will take roughly a googol (10^100) years to completely evaporate away.
After black holes evaporate, the universe enters the Dark Era, consisting of a dilute gas of particles like photons and leptons that rarely interact.
Heat death does not mean maximum heat; it represents a state of maximum entropy and thermal equilibrium where no temperature differences remain to perform work.

disputed: Certainty of Milky Way and Andromeda collision: S5 presents the galactic merger as definite, whereas S1 cites recent 2025 Gaia and Hubble observations indicating only a 50% probability within the next 10 billion years. Script should say they 'may collide' or 'are projected to merge'.

Proton decay: S1 and S5 describe matter decaying into radiation via proton decay over 10^30 to 10^40 years, but S1 notes proton decay remains unproven experimentally. Script should frame proton decay as theoretical ('if protons decay').

Final temperature of heat death: S3 and S7 describe the final temperature as hovering just above absolute zero, while S2 notes that if the cosmological constant is positive, the temperature asymptotes to a non-zero positive value. Script should focus on thermal equilibrium rather than a specific temperature number.
